prompt: Ninety-eight apples who always lie and one banana who always tells the truth are randomly arranged along a line. The first fruit says "One of the first forty fruit is the banana!" The last fruit responds "No, one of the last forty fruit is the banana!" The fruit in the middle yells "I'm the banana!" In how many positions could the banana be?

solutions.title: Case analysis
solutions.body:
There are $99$ fruit and the middle one is number $50$. Whatever it says, its claim is consistent with either identity, so it never rules out a position: ignore it.

- The banana is the first fruit: its statement is true, and the last fruit (an apple) lies since the banana is not among the last forty. Valid. Symmetrically, the banana can be the last fruit. That is $2$ positions.
- Both the first and the last fruit are apples, so both lie: the banana is not among the first $40$ and not among the last $40$, i.e. it is in positions $41,\dots,59$, which is $19$ positions.

Total $2+19=21$.

**Answer: 21**

prompt: Compute the number of ways to rearrange nine white cubes and eighteen black cubes into a $3\times3\times3$ cube such that each $1\times1\times3$ row or column contains exactly one white cube. Note that rotations are considered distinct.

solutions.title: Layer by layer
solutions.body:
Cut the cube into three horizontal $3\times3$ layers. In a layer, each of its three rows and three columns is a $1\times1\times3$ line, so it needs exactly one white cube: the three white cubes of a layer form a permutation matrix, in $3!=6$ ways for the first layer.

The vertical lines (one cell from each layer) must also contain exactly one white cube each. There are $9$ vertical lines and $9$ white cubes, so the white cubes of the three layers must occupy different cells. Given the first layer, the second layer is a permutation matrix disjoint from it: $2$ ways (a derangement-type choice of the other two permutations). The third layer is then forced: $1$ way.

Total $6\cdot2\cdot1=12$ (these are the $3\times3$ Latin squares).

**Answer: 12**

prompt: Michelle is at the bottom-left corner of a $6\times6$ lattice grid, at $(0,0)$. The grid also contains a pair of one-time-use teleportation devices at $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$; the first time Michelle moves to one of these points she is instantly teleported to the other point and the devices disappear. If she can only move up or to the right in unit increments, in how many ways can she reach the point $(5,5)$?

solutions.title: Split by which device is used
solutions.body:
Case 1: she first steps on $(2,2)$ and is teleported to $(3,3)$. Paths $(0,0)\to(2,2)$: $\binom42=6$. Paths $(3,3)\to(5,5)$: $\binom42=6$. Total $36$.

Case 2: she first steps on $(3,3)$ (avoiding $(2,2)$) and is teleported to $(2,2)$. Paths $(0,0)\to(3,3)$: $\binom63=20$, of which $\binom42\binom21=12$ pass through $(2,2)$, leaving $8$. Then $(2,2)\to(5,5)$ has $\binom63=20$ paths. Total $8\cdot20=160$.

Case 3: she steps on neither point. All paths: $\binom{10}5=252$. Through $(2,2)$: $6\cdot20=120$. Through $(3,3)$: $20\cdot6=120$. Through both: $6\cdot2\cdot6=72$. By inclusion-exclusion: $252-120-120+72=84$.

Sum: $36+160+84=280$.

**Answer: 280**

prompt: At CMU, the A and the B buses arrive once every $20$ and $18$ minutes, respectively. Kevin prefers the A bus but does not want to wait for too long. He commits to the following waiting scheme: he will take the first A bus that arrives, but after waiting for five minutes he will take the next bus that comes, no matter what it is. Determine the probability that he ends up on an A bus.

solutions.title: Geometric probability
solutions.body:
Let $a\in[0,20]$ and $b\in[0,18]$ be the times until the next A and the next B bus; they are independent and uniform, so the sample space is a $20\times18$ rectangle of area $360$.

If $a\le5$, Kevin takes the A bus. If $a>5$, at time $5$ he takes whichever bus comes next. The next B bus after time $5$ arrives at time $b$ if $b>5$, and at $b+18$ if $b\le5$. He ends up on a B bus exactly when that time is smaller than $a$:

- $5<b<a$: the area is $\int_5^{18}(20-b)\,db=110.5$;
- $b\le5$ and $b+18<a\le20$: this needs $b<2$ and has area $\int_0^2(2-b)\,db=2$.

Total B-region: $112.5=\frac12\cdot15^2$. So $P(\text{B})=\frac{112.5}{360}=\frac5{16}$ and $P(\text{A})=1-\frac5{16}=\frac{11}{16}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{11}{16}$**

prompt: Victor shuffles a standard $54$-card deck then flips over cards one at a time onto a pile stopping after the first ace. However, if he ever reveals a joker he discards the entire pile, including the joker, and starts a new pile; for example, if the sequence of cards is 2-3-Joker-A, the pile ends with one card in it. Find the expected number of cards in the end pile.

solutions.title: Use the special cards
solutions.body:
Call the four aces and two jokers special cards; the other $48$ cards are ordinary. Suppose the first ace is the $i$-th special card to appear. All earlier special cards are jokers, and the last one of them (the $(i-1)$-th special card, or the top of the deck if $i=1$) starts the final pile. The final pile therefore consists of the ordinary cards between the $(i-1)$-th and $i$-th special cards, plus the ace itself.

The six special cards cut the $48$ ordinary cards into $7$ gaps, and by symmetry each gap has expected size $\frac{48}7$. The order of the special cards (which ones are aces) is independent of the gap sizes, so whatever $i$ is, the expected pile size is $1+\frac{48}7=\frac{55}7$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{55}{7}$**

prompt: Richard rolls a fair six-sided die repeatedly until he rolls his twentieth prime number or his second even number. Compute the probability that his last roll is prime.

solutions.title: Count the ways the last roll is not prime
solutions.body:
Ignore rolls of $1$ (they change nothing), so each relevant roll is uniform on $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$. Note that $2$ is both prime and even. The last roll is not prime exactly when the game ends because the second even number is a $4$ or a $6$ (and the twentieth prime has not yet occurred).

Then the sequence is: some rolls from $\{3,5\}$ (each with probability $\frac25$), a first even roll $e$, more rolls from $\{3,5\}$, and finally a $4$ or $6$ (probability $\frac25$). Let $s$ be the total number of $3$/$5$ rolls; there are $s+1$ ways to split them around $e$, each with probability $\left(\frac25\right)^s$. The primes before the last roll number $s$ plus one more if $e=2$, and this must be at most $19$.

- $e\in\{4,6\}$ (probability $\frac25$): $s\le19$.
- $e=2$ (probability $\frac15$): $s\le18$.

With $T(M)=\sum_{s=0}^{M}(s+1)\left(\frac25\right)^s$,

$$P(\text{last roll not prime})=\frac25\left(\frac25T(19)+\frac15T(18)\right),$$

so $P(\text{prime})=1-\text{that}=\frac13+\frac{19\cdot2^{21}}{3\cdot5^{20}}=\frac{31789157162171}{5^{20}}$. This agrees with a direct dynamic-programming computation over (primes so far, evens so far) and a simulation ($\approx0.333$).

**Answer: $\dfrac{31789157162171}{95367431640625}\approx0.3333$**

solutions.title: Remark on the official key
solutions.body: The official solution assumes the game can only end after $k=20$ or $k+1=21$ rolls, giving $\frac{111\cdot2^{18}}{5^{20}}\approx3\times10^{-7}$. But the game can also end early with the second even number being a $2$, which is prime (for example the rolls $4,2$ or $2,2$), so those cases add the main contribution to the probability.

reviewNote: The official key is 111*2^18/5^20, which only counts games lasting 20 or 21 rolls and misses games ending early when the second even number is a 2 (prime, e.g. rolls 4,2). Under the literal reading (2 is both prime and even) the correct probability is 31789157162171/5^20 (confirmed by exact DP and simulation). The official value is kept as an accepted answer.

prompt: Nine distinct light bulbs are placed in a circle, each of which is off. Determine the number of ways to turn on some of the light bulbs in the circle such that no four consecutive bulbs are all off.

solutions.title: Count by the span of the on bulbs
solutions.body:
Number the bulbs $1,\dots,9$ around the circle. Let $f(n)$ be the number of configurations of $n$ bulbs in a line, with the first and last bulb on and no four consecutive bulbs off. Then $f(1)=1$ and, looking at the previous on bulb (at most $4$ places back), $f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2)+f(n-3)+f(n-4)$ (with $f(k)=0$ for $k\le0$): $f(6)=15$, $f(7)=29$, $f(8)=56$, $f(9)=108$.

In a valid circular configuration let $i$ be the first and $j$ the last bulb that is on (in the numbering $1..9$). The off bulbs wrapping around from $j$ to $i$ number at most $3$, so $j-i+1\ge6$. The span of length $L=j-i+1$ can sit in $10-L$ positions and has $f(L)$ internal configurations:

$$1\cdot f(9)+2\cdot f(8)+3\cdot f(7)+4\cdot f(6)=108+112+87+60=367.$$

**Answer: 367**

solutions.title: Direct enumeration
solutions.body: Checking all $2^9=512$ on/off patterns by computer for the condition "every four cyclically consecutive bulbs contain an on bulb" also gives $367$.

prompt: Fred and George play a game, as follows. Initially, $x=1$. Each turn, they pick $r\in\{3,5,8,9\}$ uniformly at random and multiply $x$ by $r$. If $x+1$ is a multiple of $13$, Fred wins; if $x+3$ is a multiple of $13$, George wins; otherwise, they repeat. Determine the probability that Fred wins the game.

solutions.title: Random walk on a torus
solutions.body:
Work modulo $13$. Here $9=3^{-1}$ and $8=5^{-1}$, and $3$ has order $3$, $5$ has order $4$. Every nonzero residue is $3^i5^j$ ($i\in\mathbb Z_3$, $j\in\mathbb Z_4$), and each step moves one unit up/down/left/right on the $3\times4$ torus:

$$\begin{array}{cccc}1&5&12&8\\3&2&10&11\\9&6&4&7\end{array}$$

Fred wins at $12$ ($x+1\equiv0$), George at $10$ ($x+3\equiv0$). Let $f(n)$ be Fred's winning probability from $n$. Then $f(12)=1$, $f(10)=0$. The reflection swapping rows $1$ and $2$ of the picture (fixing the bottom row) swaps the two targets, so $f(x)+f(\bar x)=1$, and the bottom row $9,6,4,7$ has $f=\frac12$. Also left-right symmetry gives $f(5)=f(8)$, $f(2)=f(11)$, and $f(3)=1-f(1)$, $f(2)=1-f(5)$.

The averaging equations at $1$ and $5$:

$$f(1)=\tfrac14\bigl(f(3)+f(9)+f(5)+f(8)\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(\tfrac32-f(1)+2f(5)\bigr),$$
$$f(5)=\tfrac14\bigl(f(1)+f(12)+f(2)+f(6)\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(f(1)+\tfrac52-f(5)\bigr).$$

So $5f(1)=\frac32+2f(5)$ and $5f(5)=f(1)+\frac52$, giving $f(5)=\frac{14}{23}$ and $f(1)=\frac{25}{46}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{46}$**

prompt: Compute the number of rearrangements $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{2018}$ of the sequence $1,2,\dots,2018$ such that $a_k>k$ for exactly one value of $k$.

solutions.title: Cycle structure
solutions.body:
View the rearrangement as a permutation $\sigma$ with $\sigma(k)=a_k$. Every cycle that is not a fixed point has at least one $k$ with $\sigma(k)>k$ (otherwise $c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_m>c_1$ around the cycle, impossible). So there is exactly one non-trivial cycle, and in it exactly one step goes up: it must be written $(b_1\,b_2\,\cdots\,b_\ell)$ with $b_1>b_2>\cdots>b_\ell$, i.e. $\sigma(b_i)=b_{i+1}$ and $\sigma(b_\ell)=b_1$. All other elements are fixed.

Conversely any such permutation works. Hence the permutations correspond to subsets of $\{1,\dots,2018\}$ with at least $2$ elements (the elements of the cycle), and there are $2^{2018}-1-2018=2^{2018}-2019$ of them. (This is the Eulerian number $2^n-n-1$ for exactly one ascent-type position; small cases $n=1,\dots,7$ give $0,1,4,11,26,57,120$.)

**Answer: $2^{2018}-2019$**

prompt: Call a set $S\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,14\}$ sparse if $x+1\pmod{15}$ is not in $S$ whenever $x\in S$. Find the number of sparse sets $T$ such that the sum of the elements of $T$ is a multiple of $15$.

solutions.title: Necklaces
solutions.body:
Claim: for odd $n$, the number of subsets of $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with sum divisible by $n$ equals the number of necklaces of $n$ black/white beads (up to rotation). For prime $n$: a nonempty proper subset $S$ has $|S|$ coprime to $n$, and shifting every element by $1$ (mod $n$) changes the sum by $|S|$, so exactly one of the $n$ rotations of $S$ has sum $\equiv0$; the empty and full sets are fixed and have sum $0$. For composite $n$ (here $15$) the same idea works after a small adjustment of the $d$ identical rotations when $|S|=d$ divides $n$, as in the official solution (and the final count is confirmed below by direct enumeration). Being sparse is preserved by rotation, so the answer is the number of necklaces of $15$ beads with no two adjacent white beads.

Circular binary strings of length $m$ with no two adjacent $1$s: $f(m)$ equals the Lucas number: $f(1)=1,f(3)=4,f(5)=11,f(15)=1364$. By Burnside's lemma the number of necklaces is

$$\frac1{15}\sum_{d\mid15}\varphi(d)f\!\left(\tfrac{15}d\right)=\frac{1364+2\cdot11+4\cdot4+8\cdot1}{15}=\frac{1410}{15}=94.$$

**Answer: 94**

solutions.title: Direct enumeration
solutions.body: Enumerating all sparse subsets of $\{0,\dots,14\}$ ($1364$ of them) and keeping those with sum divisible by $15$ gives $94$.
